title: Stop Doing forearm extensors Wrong: Train Your extensor tendons Instead
description: Snapping a band twice a month when your elbow already hurts is the wrong way to train extensors. Here is the spread test, the daily balance method that actually builds the opening system, and the slow lowering work that turns extensor tendons into elbow insurance.

scenes.narration: Here is your test again, because it is the exam for this whole system. Rubber band around all five fingertips, thumb included. Spread wide against the band, fully open, close, repeat, and count the clean spreads in thirty seconds. That number is your opening system's report card. Last time, we listed the mistakes. Today is about method, because almost everyone who does train extensors trains them backwards: too hard, too rare, and only once the elbow is already complaining. Keep your number. At the end of this video I will show you the daily balance method that builds this system properly, before it ever has to complain.

scenes.label: THE THIRTY-SPREAD LINE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Thirty clean, full spreads in thirty seconds. Under fifteen, the opening system is asleep and your forearm is a one-sided tool. Fifteen to twenty-four: waking, but the balance is not there yet. Twenty-five to twenty-nine: BALANCED, front and back sharing the work like partners. Thirty: WIRED openers, and a wrist that stays straight under any grip you own. The goal of the right way is not just this number. It is what the number protects: an elbow that never has to send you the bill for years of one-sided training.

The wrong way has a recognisable shape. A guy reads that extensors matter, buys the stiffest band he can find, and does one heroic session of snapping spreads until the back of his forearm burns like wire. Then nothing for three weeks. Then, when his elbow aches after heavy gripping, another heroic session, as if the ache were a battery to recharge. Tendons do not work like batteries. They work like gardens: small waterings, constantly, or nothing grows. The extensor tendons are thin, their blood supply is modest, and they adapt to what repeats daily, not what ambushes them monthly. The elbow deserves its own paragraph, because it is where this system's bill arrives. The extensor tendons anchor on a small bony point on the outer elbow, the lateral epicondyle, and every grip you make tugs that anchor through the wrist extensors. When the extensors are weak, the tug concentrates. When they are strong and enduring, the load spreads across a trained team. This is why the spread test predicts elbow trouble better than any squeeze test: it measures the very team standing between your gripping habit and that bony anchor.

The right way starts with a downgrade that feels like cheating: a LIGHTER band. With a light band you can do the two things that actually build this system. First, full range, spreading to a complete open with the fingers straight, not a three-quarter shrug. Second, the slow return: closing against the band over three full seconds, the extensor tendons lengthening under control. That lowering phase, the eccentric, is where tendon tissue takes its strongest building signal, the same lesson your Achilles and your elbows keep teaching in every season of this channel. There is also a quiet performance dividend nobody mentions. A strong opening system makes your grip RELAX faster between efforts. Watch a climber shake out on a rest hold: the hand opens wide, blood rushes back, and the next grip starts full. That shake is extensor work doing double duty, clearing the forearm while the flexors rest. Train the openers and every grip sport you play gets longer rests hidden inside it. Your hangs, carries and climbs all quietly extend, paid for by five minutes with a rubber band.

The second movement of the right way is the wrist extension hold. Forearm resting on a table, hand off the edge, light weight or a water bottle in hand, raise the back of the hand toward the ceiling and hold. This loads the wrist extensors in their stabilising job, the exact job they do when your wrist stays straight during a heavy grip. Thirty seconds a side, a few times a day, while you work or watch anything. It is the least heroic exercise on this channel, and for elbow longevity it might be the most valuable one we have ever programmed. If you type or game for hours, count that as part of this system too. The mouse hand lives in a half-open, half-working position that tires the extensors without strengthening them, a debt that follows you into training. A few spreads every hour at the desk is not a distraction from the method. For desk workers it IS the method, the highest-frequency version of it, and their spread numbers often jump fastest of all in the first month.

beats.title: STABILISER TRAINING
lines: Extension holds load the wrist's guy-wires.
They protect every heavy grip you make.

scenes.narration: Dosage is the whole method, so write this down. Two to five minutes of extensor work, DAILY, at an effort that feels almost too easy. Band spreads while the kettle boils. Extension holds during calls. The system you are building is a background system, and it grows on background training. Save the intensity for your flexors and your hangs. The extensors are not a workout. They are a habit, like brushing your teeth, and like teeth, you only notice them when the habit was skipped for years.

beats.title: 2-5 MINUTES, DAILY
lines: Light band, full range, slow return.
Too easy is exactly right here.

scenes.narration: Your advantage in this system is that it is beneath everyone's notice. The big guys will not do it; it looks like rehab and smells like weakness, and their elbows will collect the debt in their thirties and forties. You, with your desk-friendly band and your five quiet minutes, are building the balanced forearms they will wish they had, at the exact age when balance starts deciding who still trains hard. Skinny guys do not win by out-lifting anyone. They win by still being uninjured, and training, when the room has emptied.
Spread with me, the right way. Thirty seconds: full opens, three-second closes, light band. Thirty seconds rest, four rounds. If it feels too easy, you are doing it perfectly. Go.

So here is the right way, as a checklist. Light band, never the stiffest. Full range on every rep, fingers straight at the open. Three-second closings, because the lowering is the lesson. Two to five minutes daily, attached to habits you already have. Extension holds a few times a day for the stabilisers. And one rule that outranks the method: if your outer elbow develops a persistent ache, do not hero through it with more band work. Ease off the gripping, keep the gentle work, and if the pain persists, see a professional and get a proper assessment. The method is insurance. Insurance only works if you buy it before the fire.

So, your spread number. Under fifteen: asleep, and the daily method will wake it inside a month. Fifteen to twenty-four: BUILDING, balance arriving. Twenty-five to twenty-nine: balanced, the partnership working. Thirty clean: WIRED openers, with elbows built to last. Put your reps in the comments, just the number. In thirty days we spread again, and the back of your forearm, the half nobody trains, will have doubled its testimony.
Thirty days of quiet daily spreads, and the system you ignored will start paying rent. Subscribe, because every week we test another cable the mirror cannot see. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
